title: The great vehicle
hookLine: the name the Mahayana gave itself; Buddhists today avoid the old contrast term and say Theravada instead

cards: A big old house is on fire, and the father is outside. His children are still in there, playing, too absorbed to notice the smoke. He shouts, and they don't come.
So he tries something else. He calls out that carts are waiting at the gate, the kind they've always wanted: one pulled by goats, one by deer, one by an ox. The children come running out.

And when they're safe, he doesn't give them those three. He gives each child one great cart, finer than any of them asked for. That story comes from the Lotus Sutra, and its word for those carts is in today's name.

teach.h: YANA: A CART, A WAY ACROSS.
teach.b: You met these sutras arriving on day eight hundred seventy-five. Today, their name. First, the vehicle.
The Sanskrit word is yana: a cart, a vehicle, the thing that carries you somewhere. Buddhist teachers used it for a path, the way across.
In the parable, the three carts stand for different paths of practice, and the one great cart for the single vehicle the sutra says they all lead into. Second, the name.
Communities who treasured sutras like the Lotus called their way Mahayana.
Maha means great: the great vehicle, wide enough to carry all beings. That's the name they gave themselves, and it's the name used here. Third, the hard part.

teach.h: AN OLD CONTRAST WORD, SET DOWN.
teach.b: Some Mahayana texts also used a contrast term for other paths: a lesser, or small, vehicle. It was a word for someone else, not a name anyone took for themselves.
The Buddhists of Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia call their own tradition Theravada, the way of the elders.
Buddhists today avoid the old contrast term and say Theravada instead, and so will this path; when the old term shows up in a text, it's there as history. Fourth, what that habit teaches.
A name someone gives you can carry a judgment inside it. A name you give yourself carries what you love.
Mahayana, Theravada, and the schools ahead on this path, Zen, Pure Land, the Tibetan traditions, will each be called here by the name they use. No ranking, just each by its own name.

how: Mahayana is the name used for the Buddhist traditions of China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam and Tibet, among others; Buddhists today refer to the tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia as Theravada.

o: the great vehicle, wide enough for all beings
the great vow a monk takes at ordination
the great council where the canon was fixed

games.q: each by its own name: tap the pairs.
p: a cart, a vehicle, a way across
a parable in the Lotus Sutra
the way of the elders, its own name

s: Mahayana is a name other people gave these communities
it's the name they gave their own way: the great vehicle.
in the parable, the father gives each child one great cart
he promised goat, deer and ox carts, and gave each child one finer cart.
the old contrast term is the name Theravada Buddhists use for themselves
it was a word for someone else. their own name is Theravada, the way of the elders.

games.q: your children are playing in a burning house and won't come out when you shout. what does the father in the Lotus Sutra do?
o: run in and carry them out one by one
promise the carts they've always wanted
games.why: he promises goat, deer and ox carts at the gate. they come running, and then he gives each one great cart instead.

practice: Bring to mind a few people you know, one at a time, and notice the name you use for each in your head: the name they'd use, a nickname they never liked, or a label like the difficult one.
Gently swap it for the name they'd choose, say it silently, and let their face come with it.

wordCard.voice: Mahayana. The great vehicle: the name these communities gave their own way, wide enough to carry all beings. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: maha, great, and yana, vehicle. the great vehicle.

carryVoice: Your line: each by its own name. One great cart, wide enough to carry all beings. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Saddharma-pundarika (Lotus Sutra), chapter 3, the parable of the burning house (Kern, SBE XXI, 1884)
